questions.question: A metal electrode is constructed by dipping a metal rod into an aqueous solution containing its ions. The electrode potential of this half-cell is independent of the:
options: surface area of the metal rod
concentration of the metal ions in the solution
questions.solution:
The electrode potential of a metal half-cell is given by the Nernst equation:

$E = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{RT}{nF} \ln \dfrac{1}{[M^{n+}]}$

The standard electrode potential $E^{\circ}$ depends on the nature of the metal.

The equation shows that the electrode potential $E$ depends on the temperature $T$ and the concentration of the metal ions $[M^{n+}]$.

The activity of a pure solid metal is taken as unity, which means the electrode potential does not depend on the amount or the surface area of the solid metal rod present.

Therefore, the electrode potential is independent of the surface area of the metal rod.

Answer: surface area of the metal rod

Given the standard reduction potentials: $E^\circ_{\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al}} = -1.66\text{ V}$ and $E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}$.
What will happen when a copper spoon is used to stir an aqueous solution of aluminium nitrate?
questions.question:
Given the standard reduction potentials: $E^\circ_{\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al}} = -1.66\text{ V}$ and $E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}$.
What will happen when a copper spoon is used to stir an aqueous solution of aluminium nitrate?
options: The solution will turn blue due to the formation of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions.
An alloy of copper and aluminium will be formed.
The spoon will get coated with solid aluminium.
No chemical change will take place.
questions.solution:
The standard reduction potential of aluminium ($E^\circ_{\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al}} = -1.66\text{ V}$) is lower than that of copper ($E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}$).

This indicates that aluminium is a stronger reducing agent and is more reactive than copper.

For a reaction to occur between the copper spoon and aluminium nitrate solution, copper would have to displace aluminium from the solution:

$3\text{Cu} + 2\text{Al}^{3+} \rightarrow 3\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{Al}$

The standard cell potential for this reaction is:

$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} = -1.66\text{ V} - 0.34\text{ V} = -2.00\text{ V}$

Since $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ is negative, the reaction is non-spontaneous.

Therefore, a less reactive metal (copper) cannot displace a more reactive metal (aluminium) from its salt solution, and no chemical change will take place.

Answer: No chemical change will take place.

questions.question: A piece of copper wire is added to four separate beakers containing colourless aqueous solutions of different metal nitrates. The solution in one of the beakers gradually turns blue. The salt present in this beaker is:
questions.solution:
Copper is placed above silver in the electrochemical series, which means copper is more reactive than silver and has a lower standard reduction potential ($E^{\circ}_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}$, $E^{\circ}_{\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}$).

When a piece of copper wire is added to a colourless silver nitrate solution, copper displaces silver from the solution.

The chemical reaction is:
$\text{Cu(s)} + 2\text{AgNO}_3\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Cu(NO}_3)_2\text{(aq)} + 2\text{Ag(s)}$

The solution gradually turns blue due to the formation of copper(II) nitrate, which contains blue-coloured $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions in aqueous solution.

Copper cannot displace zinc, lead, or barium from their respective nitrate solutions because these metals are placed above copper in the reactivity series (they have negative standard reduction potentials).

Answer: $\text{AgNO}_3$

Therefore, no chemical reaction will take place.

questions.q: The standard electrode potential of the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) is taken as zero at all temperatures. This is because:
questions.question: The standard electrode potential of the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) is taken as zero at all temperatures. This is because:
options: the absolute potential of the hydrogen half-cell is experimentally measured to be exactly zero.
hydrogen ion ($\text{H}^+$) has the highest hydration enthalpy among all cations.
hydrogen is the lightest element and easily undergoes oxidation.
it is arbitrarily assigned a value of zero by convention to act as a reference.
questions.solution:
The absolute value of the electrode potential of a single half-cell cannot be measured experimentally because a half-cell reaction cannot take place independently.

To measure the relative electrode potentials of various half-cells, a reference electrode is required. By international convention, the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) is chosen as the primary reference electrode.

Its standard electrode potential is arbitrarily assigned a value of exactly zero volts at all temperatures. This allows the standard electrode potentials of all other electrodes to be measured relative to it.

Answer: it is arbitrarily assigned a value of zero by convention to act as a reference.

The standard reduction potentials for the half-reactions $\dfrac{1}{2} X_2 + e^- \rightarrow X^-$ (where $X = P, Q, R$) follow the order $R > Q > P$. Which of the following statements is correct regarding their redox behaviour under standard conditions?
questions.solution:
The standard reduction potentials for the given half-reactions follow the order $R > Q > P$.

A higher standard reduction potential implies a stronger tendency for the species to get reduced, which makes it a stronger oxidizing agent. Therefore, the oxidizing power of the non-metals follows the order $R_2 > Q_2 > P_2$.

A stronger oxidizing agent can oxidize the anion of a non-metal that has a lower reduction potential.

Based on the order of oxidizing power:
$R_2$ can oxidize both $Q^-$ and $P^-$.
$Q_2$ can oxidize $P^-$ but cannot oxidize $R^-$.
$P_2$ cannot oxidize either $Q^-$ or $R^-$.

Thus, $Q_2$ will oxidize $P^-$ but not $R^-$.

Answer: $Q_2$ will oxidize $P^-$ but not $R^-$.

$\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} (\text{aq}) + 14\text{H}^+ (\text{aq}) + 6\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})$$1.38$

Identify the incorrect statement regarding the quantitative estimation of aqueous $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ions.
questions.question:

Half-cell reaction$E^\circ$ (V)

$\text{Fe}^{3+} (\text{aq}) + \text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+} (\text{aq})$$0.77$
Identify the incorrect statement regarding the quantitative estimation of aqueous $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ions.
options: $\text{KMnO}_4$ can be used for titration in aqueous $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ medium.
$\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ can be used for titration in aqueous $\text{HCl}$ medium.
$\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ can be used for titration in aqueous $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ medium.
$\text{KMnO}_4$ can be used for titration in aqueous $\text{HCl}$ medium.
questions.solution:
For the quantitative estimation of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$, the oxidant must oxidize $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ without oxidizing the anion of the acid used as the medium.

The standard reduction potential of $\text{MnO}_4^- / \text{Mn}^{2+}$ is $1.51\text{ V}$, which is greater than that of $\text{Cl}_2 / \text{Cl}^-$ ($1.40\text{ V}$). Thus, $\text{MnO}_4^-$ will oxidize $\text{Cl}^-$ to $\text{Cl}_2$ along with oxidizing $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$. This will consume extra $\text{KMnO}_4$, leading to an erroneous estimation of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$. Therefore, $\text{KMnO}_4$ cannot be used for titration in aqueous $\text{HCl}$ medium.

The standard reduction potential of $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} / \text{Cr}^{3+}$ is $1.38\text{ V}$, which is less than $1.40\text{ V}$. Thus, $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ does not oxidize $\text{Cl}^-$ to $\text{Cl}_2$ and can be safely used in aqueous $\text{HCl}$ medium.

Both oxidants can be used in aqueous $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ medium as the $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ion is not oxidized by them.

Hence, the statement that $\text{KMnO}_4$ can be used for titration in aqueous $\text{HCl}$ medium is incorrect.

Answer: $\text{KMnO}_4$ can be used for titration in aqueous $\text{HCl}$ medium.

questions.question: When a metal with a negative standard reduction potential is dipped in a $1 \text{ M}$ aqueous solution of its own ions at $298 \text{ K}$, it shows a tendency to:
options: undergo reduction, resulting in a positively charged metal electrode.
undergo reduction, resulting in a negatively charged metal electrode.
undergo oxidation, resulting in a positively charged metal electrode.
undergo oxidation, resulting in a negatively charged metal electrode.
questions.solution:
A negative standard reduction potential indicates that the metal has a higher tendency to undergo oxidation than reduction when compared to the standard hydrogen electrode.

The oxidation reaction is given by $M(s) \rightarrow M^{n+}(aq) + ne^{-}$.

As the metal atoms lose electrons and enter the solution as positive ions, the electrons are left behind on the metal rod.

This accumulation of electrons makes the metal electrode negatively charged.

Thus, the metal shows a tendency to undergo oxidation, resulting in a negatively charged metal electrode.

Answer: undergo oxidation, resulting in a negatively charged metal electrode.

questions.q: The calomel electrode is a commonly used secondary reference electrode. Its half-cell potential is reversible with respect to the concentration of which of the following ions?
questions.question: The calomel electrode is a commonly used secondary reference electrode. Its half-cell potential is reversible with respect to the concentration of which of the following ions?
questions.solution:
The calomel electrode consists of mercury, solid mercury(I) chloride ($\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$), and a solution of potassium chloride ($\text{KCl}$).

The half-cell reaction is given by:
$\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2(s) + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Hg}(l) + 2\text{Cl}^-(aq)$

The Nernst equation for this electrode is:
$E = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{RT}{2F} \ln [\text{Cl}^-]^2 = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{RT}{F} \ln [\text{Cl}^-]$

From the equation, the electrode potential depends only on the concentration of chloride ions ($\text{Cl}^-$). Thus, the half-cell potential is reversible with respect to the concentration of $\text{Cl}^-$ ions.

Answer: $\text{Cl}^-$

Bromine water acts as an oxidizing agent, meaning it undergoes reduction at the cathode. Thus, $E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^-} = +1.09 \text{ V}$.

For the oxidation of $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ to $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$, the anode potential is $E^{\circ}_{\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}/\text{Cr}^{3+}} = +1.33 \text{ V}$.

$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 1.09 \text{ V} - 1.33 \text{ V} = -0.24 \text{ V}$

Since $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}$ is negative, this reaction is non-spontaneous. Bromine water cannot oxidize $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ to $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$.

For the other conversions, the standard reduction potentials are lower than $+1.09 \text{ V}$, resulting in a positive $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}$:
$\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$: $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 1.09 - 0.77 = +0.32 \text{ V}$
$\text{I}^-$ to $\text{I}_2$: $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 1.09 - 0.54 = +0.55 \text{ V}$
$\text{Sn}^{2+}$ to $\text{Sn}^{4+}$: $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 1.09 - 0.15 = +0.94 \text{ V}$

Answer: $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ to $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$

questions.q: An aqueous solution of $\text{KCl}$ in agar-agar is frequently preferred as the electrolyte in a salt bridge for galvanic cells. The primary reason for selecting $\text{KCl}$ is that:
questions.question: An aqueous solution of $\text{KCl}$ in agar-agar is frequently preferred as the electrolyte in a salt bridge for galvanic cells. The primary reason for selecting $\text{KCl}$ is that:
options: both $\text{K}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions undergo extensive hydration in aqueous medium.
the ionic mobilities of $\text{K}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions are nearly equal.
$\text{KCl}$ is a strong electrolyte that completely dissociates into ions.
it provides a physical barrier that prevents the mixing of the two half-cell solutions.
questions.solution:
The primary function of a salt bridge in a galvanic cell is to maintain electrical neutrality in the two half-cells and to minimize the liquid junction potential.

To achieve this, the electrolyte used in the salt bridge must have cations and anions with nearly equal ionic mobilities (or transport numbers).

In the case of $\text{KCl}$, the ionic mobilities of $\text{K}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions are almost identical. This ensures that they migrate at the same rate into the respective half-cells, effectively neutralizing the charge without creating an additional potential difference.

Therefore, $\text{KCl}$ is frequently preferred as the electrolyte in a salt bridge.

Answer: the ionic mobilities of $\text{K}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions are nearly equal.

questions.q:
Consider the half-reactions and their standard reduction potentials at $298\text{ K}$ given below:
Half-reaction$E^{\circ} \text{ (V)}$
$\text{MnO}_4^- + 8\text{H}^+ + 5\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$1.51$
$\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$1.33$

If the concentration of $\text{H}^+$ ions in a half-cell containing the $\text{MnO}_4^- / \text{Mn}^{2+}$ couple is decreased by a factor of $100$ at $298\text{ K}$ (keeping the concentrations of all other species constant), the magnitude of change in its reduction potential is ______ $\text{mV}$. (Nearest integer)

[Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}$]
questions.question:
Consider the half-reactions and their standard reduction potentials at $298\text{ K}$ given below:
Half-reaction$E^{\circ} \text{ (V)}$
$\text{MnO}_4^- + 8\text{H}^+ + 5\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$1.51$
$\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$1.33$

If the concentration of $\text{H}^+$ ions in a half-cell containing the $\text{MnO}_4^- / \text{Mn}^{2+}$ couple is decreased by a factor of $100$ at $298\text{ K}$ (keeping the concentrations of all other species constant), the magnitude of change in its reduction potential is ______ $\text{mV}$. (Nearest integer)

[Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}$]
questions.solution:
The given half-reaction is:

$\text{MnO}_4^- + 8\text{H}^+ + 5\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$

The Nernst equation for the reduction potential of this half-cell is:

$E = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{0.059}{5} \log \dfrac{[\text{Mn}^{2+}]}{[\text{MnO}_4^-][\text{H}^+]^8}$

Using the property of logarithms, this can be rewritten as:

$E = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{0.059}{5} \log \dfrac{[\text{Mn}^{2+}]}{[\text{MnO}_4^-]} + \dfrac{0.059 \times 8}{5} \log [\text{H}^+]$

When the concentration of $\text{H}^+$ ions is decreased by a factor of $100$, the new concentration becomes $[\text{H}^+]' = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+]}{100} = 10^{-2}[\text{H}^+]$.

The new reduction potential $E'$ is:

$E' = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{0.059}{5} \log \dfrac{[\text{Mn}^{2+}]}{[\text{MnO}_4^-]} + \dfrac{0.059 \times 8}{5} \log (10^{-2}[\text{H}^+])$

$E' = E + \dfrac{0.059 \times 8}{5} \log (10^{-2})$

The change in reduction potential $\Delta E$ is:

$\Delta E = E' - E = \dfrac{0.059 \times 8}{5} \times (-2)$

$\Delta E = -\dfrac{0.944}{5} = -0.1888 \text{ V}$

The magnitude of the change in reduction potential is $0.1888 \text{ V}$, which is equal to $188.8 \text{ mV}$.

Rounding to the nearest integer, we get $189 \text{ mV}$.

Answer: $189$

A copper rod is immersed in an aqueous solution of $\text{CuSO}_4$ at $298 \text{ K}$. If the solution is diluted to 100 times its original volume, the reduction electrode potential of the half-cell decreases by $x \text{ mV}$. The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: $\dfrac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059 \text{ V}$)
questions.question:
A copper rod is immersed in an aqueous solution of $\text{CuSO}_4$ at $298 \text{ K}$. If the solution is diluted to 100 times its original volume, the reduction electrode potential of the half-cell decreases by $x \text{ mV}$. The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: $\dfrac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059 \text{ V}$)
questions.solution:
The half-cell reaction for the reduction of copper is:

$\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu}$

The Nernst equation for the reduction potential is given by:

$E = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{2.303RT}{nF} \log \dfrac{1}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}$

Substituting $n = 2$ and $\dfrac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059 \text{ V}$:

$E = E^{\circ} + \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log [\text{Cu}^{2+}]$

Let the initial concentration of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ be $C$. The initial reduction potential is:

$E_1 = E^{\circ} + \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log C$

When the solution is diluted to $100$ times its original volume, the new concentration becomes $\dfrac{C}{100}$. The new reduction potential is:

$E_2 = E^{\circ} + \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log \left(\dfrac{C}{100}\right)$

$E_2 = E^{\circ} + \dfrac{0.059}{2} (\log C - \log 100)$

$E_2 = E^{\circ} + \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log C - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \times 2$

$E_2 = E_1 - 0.059 \text{ V}$

The decrease in the reduction electrode potential is $0.059 \text{ V}$, which is equal to $59 \text{ mV}$.

Thus, $x = 59$.

Answer: $59$

The standard reduction potential of oxygen in acidic solution at $298\text{ K}$ is given as:
$\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + 4e^- \to 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) \quad E^\circ = +1.23\text{ V}$
The standard reduction potential for the reaction $\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) + 4e^- \to 4\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$ at $298\text{ K}$ is $x \times 10^{-3}\text{ V}$. The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}$ at $298\text{ K}$, $K_w = 1 \times 10^{-14}$)
questions.question:
The standard reduction potential of oxygen in acidic solution at $298\text{ K}$ is given as:
$\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + 4e^- \to 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) \quad E^\circ = +1.23\text{ V}$
The standard reduction potential for the reaction $\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) + 4e^- \to 4\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$ at $298\text{ K}$ is $x \times 10^{-3}\text{ V}$. The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}$ at $298\text{ K}$, $K_w = 1 \times 10^{-14}$)
questions.solution:
For the half-cell reaction in acidic medium:
$\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + 4e^- \to 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})$

The Nernst equation at $298\text{ K}$ is:
$E = E^\circ - \dfrac{0.059}{4} \log \dfrac{1}{P_{\text{O}_2} [\text{H}^+]^4}$

For the standard reduction potential in basic medium, the standard state conditions are $P_{\text{O}_2} = 1\text{ bar}$ and $[\text{OH}^-] = 1\text{ M}$.

Using the ionic product of water, $K_w = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-14}$, when $[\text{OH}^-] = 1\text{ M}$, the hydrogen ion concentration is $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-14}\text{ M}$.

Substituting these values into the Nernst equation gives the standard reduction potential for the basic medium ($E^\circ_{\text{base}}$):
$E^\circ_{\text{base}} = 1.23 - \dfrac{0.059}{4} \log \dfrac{1}{1 \times (10^{-14})^4}$

$E^\circ_{\text{base}} = 1.23 - \dfrac{0.059}{4} \log(10^{56})$

$E^\circ_{\text{base}} = 1.23 - \dfrac{0.059 \times 56}{4}$

$E^\circ_{\text{base}} = 1.23 - 14 \times 0.059$

$E^\circ_{\text{base}} = 1.23 - 0.826 = 0.404\text{ V}$

Expressing this in the required format:
$E^\circ_{\text{base}} = 404 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V}$

Therefore, $x = 404$.

Answer: $404$

questions.question:

Half-reaction$E^\circ$ (V)
$\text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}(\text{s})$$0.337$
$\text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}^+(\text{aq})$$0.153$

The standard electrode potential for the half-cell reaction $\text{Cu}^+(\text{aq}) + e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}(\text{s})$ is $x \text{ mV}$. The value of $x$ is ____.
questions.solution:
The given half-reactions are:

$\text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}(\text{s})$, $E^\circ_1 = 0.337 \text{ V}$, $\Delta G^\circ_1 = -2 F (0.337)$

$\text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}^+(\text{aq})$, $E^\circ_2 = 0.153 \text{ V}$, $\Delta G^\circ_2 = -1 F (0.153)$

The target half-reaction is:

$\text{Cu}^+(\text{aq}) + e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}(\text{s})$, $\Delta G^\circ_3 = -1 F E^\circ_3$

Subtracting the second reaction from the first gives the target reaction:

$\Delta G^\circ_3 = \Delta G^\circ_1 - \Delta G^\circ_2$

$-1 F E^\circ_3 = -2 F (0.337) - (-1 F (0.153))$

$-E^\circ_3 = -0.674 + 0.153$

$-E^\circ_3 = -0.521$

$E^\circ_3 = 0.521 \text{ V}$

Converting to millivolts:

$E^\circ_3 = 0.521 \times 1000 \text{ mV} = 521 \text{ mV}$

The value of $x$ is $521$.

Answer: $521$

questions.question:

(Given: $\dfrac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}$)
questions.solution:
The reduction half-reaction for the hydrogen electrode is:

$H^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow \dfrac{1}{2}H_{2}$

The Nernst equation for the electrode potential is:

$E = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{0.059}{1} \log \dfrac{(P_{H_{2}})^{1/2}}{[H^{+}]}$

For a neutral aqueous solution at $298\text{ K}$, $[H^{+}] = 10^{-7}\text{ M}$.

Given $P_{H_{2}} = 1\text{ bar}$ and $E^{\circ} = 0\text{ V}$, substituting these values:

$E = 0 - 0.059 \log \dfrac{1}{10^{-7}}$

$E = -0.059 \log (10^{7})$

$E = -0.059 \times 7 = -0.413\text{ V}$

The magnitude of the electrode potential is $|E| = 0.413\text{ V} = 413 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V}$.

Thus, $x = 413$.

Answer: $413$

questions.question: In a galvanic cell, a salt bridge is typically constructed using a saturated solution of electrolytes such as $\text{KNO}_3$ or $\text{KCl}$ in agar-agar. The primary reason for selecting these specific electrolytes is that:
options: the velocity of the cation is significantly greater than that of the anion.
the velocity of the anion is significantly greater than that of the cation.
they are highly soluble in water and form a concentrated solution.
the ionic mobilities of the cation and the anion are nearly the same.
questions.solution:
The primary function of a salt bridge in a galvanic cell is to maintain electrical neutrality in the half-cells and to minimize the liquid junction potential.

To achieve this, the electrolyte used in the salt bridge must have cations and anions with nearly equal ionic mobilities (or transport numbers).

In electrolytes like $\text{KNO}_3$ and $\text{KCl}$, the ionic mobilities of $\text{K}^+$ and $\text{NO}_3^-$ (or $\text{Cl}^-$) are almost the same, ensuring that ions move at similar speeds into the respective half-cells to neutralize the accumulated charges efficiently.

Answer: the ionic mobilities of the cation and the anion are nearly the same.

questions.solution:

Using the Nernst equation for the half-cell:

$E = 0 - 0.059 \log (10^{-3})$

The magnitude of the electrode potential is $0.177 \text{ V}$, which can be written as $177 \times 10^{-3} \text{ V}$.

Comparing this with $x \times 10^{-3} \text{ V}$, we get $x = 177$.

questions.question:

The standard reduction potential of the $\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}$ electrode ($E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}}$) is $x \times 10^{-2}\text{ V}$.
The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.06\text{ V}$)
questions.solution:
The reduction half-reaction for the metal-insoluble salt electrode is:
$\text{CuCl}(s) + e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}(s) + \text{Cl}^-(aq)$

This reaction can be obtained by adding the following two reactions:
1) $\text{Cu}^+(aq) + e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}(s)$
$\Delta G^\circ_1 = -n F E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}} = -1 \times F \times E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}}$

2) $\text{CuCl}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq)$
$\Delta G^\circ_2 = -2.303 R T \log K_{sp}$

Adding the two reactions gives the overall reaction for the $\text{Cl}^-|\text{CuCl}|\text{Cu}$ electrode:
$\Delta G^\circ_3 = -1 \times F \times E^\circ_{\text{Cl}^-|\text{CuCl}|\text{Cu}}$

Since $\Delta G^\circ_3 = \Delta G^\circ_1 + \Delta G^\circ_2$, we have:
$-F E^\circ_{\text{Cl}^-|\text{CuCl}|\text{Cu}} = -F E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}} - 2.303 R T \log K_{sp}$

Dividing the entire equation by $-F$ gives:
$E^\circ_{\text{Cl}^-|\text{CuCl}|\text{Cu}} = E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}} + \dfrac{2.303 R T}{F} \log K_{sp}$

Substituting the given values:
$0.10 = E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}} + 0.06 \log(1.0 \times 10^{-7})$
$0.10 = E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}} + 0.06 \times (-7)$
$0.10 = E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}} - 0.42$
$E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}} = 0.10 + 0.42 = 0.52\text{ V}$

Expressing this in the required format:
$E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}} = 52 \times 10^{-2}\text{ V}$

Comparing with $x \times 10^{-2}\text{ V}$, we get $x = 52$.

Answer: $52$

$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{Cl}^-|\text{AgCl}|\text{Ag}} - E^\circ_{\text{Zn}^{2+}|\text{Zn}}$

questions.q: In an electrochemical cell set-up, a salt bridge connects two half-cells and the cell potential is measured using a voltmeter. If the salt bridge is suddenly removed from the set-up, the voltage reading on the voltmeter will:
questions.question: In an electrochemical cell set-up, a salt bridge connects two half-cells and the cell potential is measured using a voltmeter. If the salt bridge is suddenly removed from the set-up, the voltage reading on the voltmeter will:
options: decrease gradually to half of its initial value
questions.solution:
The salt bridge in an electrochemical cell completes the internal circuit by allowing the flow of ions between the two half-cells, which maintains electrical neutrality.

If the salt bridge is suddenly removed, the internal circuit is broken. As a result, the flow of electrons in the external circuit stops instantly because the overall circuit becomes open.

Therefore, the cell stops functioning and the voltage reading on the voltmeter drops to zero immediately.

Answer: drop to zero immediately

questions.q: As a galvanic cell operates, its cell potential gradually decreases and eventually drops to zero. Which of the following statements correctly explains this observation?
questions.question: As a galvanic cell operates, its cell potential gradually decreases and eventually drops to zero. Which of the following statements correctly explains this observation?
options: The reduction potentials of the cathode and the anode become equal.
The concentrations of the electrolyte solutions in both half-cells become equal.
The reduction potentials of the cathode and the anode become equal in magnitude but opposite in sign.
The standard reduction potentials of the two half-cells become equal.
questions.solution:
The cell potential of a galvanic cell is given by $E_{cell} = E_{cathode} - E_{anode}$.

As the cell operates, the concentration of the reactant ions at the cathode decreases, which causes the reduction potential of the cathode to decrease according to the Nernst equation.

Simultaneously, the concentration of the product ions at the anode increases, which causes the reduction potential of the anode to increase.

The cell continues to operate until the reduction potentials of both the cathode and the anode become equal. At this point, $E_{cathode} = E_{anode}$, making $E_{cell} = 0$. The cell is then said to have reached equilibrium.

Answer: The reduction potentials of the cathode and the anode become equal.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding a galvanic cell:

(B) The anode of a galvanic cell is considered the positive terminal.

questions.solution:
Statement (A) is correct. In any electrochemical cell, oxidation always takes place at the anode.

Statement (B) is incorrect. In a galvanic cell, the anode is the negative terminal because electrons are generated there during oxidation.

Statement (C) is correct. By convention, the direction of electric current is taken as opposite to the direction of the flow of electrons.

Statement (D) is correct. Within the internal circuit (electrolyte and salt bridge), charge is transported by the movement of ions.

Statement (E) is incorrect. In the external circuit, electrons flow from the anode (negative terminal) to the cathode (positive terminal).

Thus, statements (A), (C), and (D) are correct.

Answer: (A), (C) and (D) only

questions.question: During the continuous operation of a simple galvanic cell, as electric current is drawn from it, the cell potential ($E_{\text{cell}}$) :
options: remains constant until the cell is completely exhausted.

questions.solution:
For a galvanic cell, the cell potential is given by the Nernst equation:

$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{RT}{nF} \ln Q$

where $Q$ is the reaction quotient, which is the ratio of the concentration of products to the concentration of reactants.

As the cell operates and current is drawn, reactants are consumed and products are formed. This causes the concentration of products to increase and the concentration of reactants to decrease, leading to a continuous increase in the value of $Q$.

As $Q$ increases, the term $\dfrac{RT}{nF} \ln Q$ also increases, which means $E_{\text{cell}}$ gradually decreases.

Eventually, the cell reaction reaches equilibrium. At equilibrium, $Q = K_{\text{eq}}$ and the cell potential $E_{\text{cell}}$ becomes zero. Thus, the cell potential gradually decreases and finally becomes zero.

Answer: gradually decreases and finally becomes zero.

If the concentrations of both $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions are doubled at $298 \text{ K}$, the change in the electromotive force (EMF) of the cell is $x \text{ mV}$. The value of $x$ is ____.
questions.question: For the galvanic cell $\text{Zn}(\text{s}) | \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq}) || \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) | \text{Cu}(\text{s})$, the initial concentrations of $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ are $C_1$ and $C_2$ respectively. If the concentrations of both $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions are doubled at $298 \text{ K}$, the change in the electromotive force (EMF) of the cell is $x \text{ mV}$. The value of $x$ is ____.
questions.solution:
The cell reaction for the given galvanic cell is:

$\text{Zn}(\text{s}) + \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + \text{Cu}(\text{s})$

The Nernst equation for the electromotive force (EMF) of the cell is:

$E = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{2.303 RT}{nF} \log \left( \dfrac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]} \right)$

For the initial state, $[\text{Zn}^{2+}] = C_1$ and $[\text{Cu}^{2+}] = C_2$. The initial EMF is:

$E_1 = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{0.0591}{2} \log \left( \dfrac{C_1}{C_2} \right)$

When the concentrations of both ions are doubled, $[\text{Zn}^{2+}] = 2C_1$ and $[\text{Cu}^{2+}] = 2C_2$. The new EMF is:

$E_2 = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{0.0591}{2} \log \left( \dfrac{2C_1}{2C_2} \right)$

$E_2 = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{0.0591}{2} \log \left( \dfrac{C_1}{C_2} \right)$

The change in EMF is:

$\Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = 0$

Therefore, the change in EMF is $0 \text{ mV}$, which gives $x = 0$.

Answer: $0$

questions.q: For a cell reaction to be feasible under standard conditions, the correct relationship among the standard cell potential ($E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$), standard Gibbs free energy change ($\Delta G^\circ$), and the equilibrium constant ($K$) is:
questions.question: For a cell reaction to be feasible under standard conditions, the correct relationship among the standard cell potential ($E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$), standard Gibbs free energy change ($\Delta G^\circ$), and the equilibrium constant ($K$) is:
questions.solution:
For a cell reaction to be feasible (spontaneous) under standard conditions, the standard Gibbs free energy change must be negative, i.e., $\Delta G^\circ < 0$.

The relationship between $\Delta G^\circ$ and standard cell potential $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ is given by $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}$.

For $\Delta G^\circ < 0$, $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ must be positive, i.e., $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} > 0$.

The relationship between $\Delta G^\circ$ and the equilibrium constant $K$ is given by $\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K$.

For $\Delta G^\circ < 0$, $\ln K$ must be positive, which means $K > 1$.

Thus, the correct relationship is $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} > 0$, $\Delta G^\circ < 0$, $K > 1$.

Answer: $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} > 0$, $\Delta G^\circ < 0$, $K > 1$

questions.q: For a galvanic cell operating under a given set of non-standard conditions, the cell reaction will be spontaneous if:
questions.question: For a galvanic cell operating under a given set of non-standard conditions, the cell reaction will be spontaneous if:
questions.solution:
For a cell reaction to be spontaneous under any given set of conditions, the change in Gibbs free energy must be negative, i.e., $\Delta G < 0$.

The relationship between the Gibbs free energy change and the cell potential is given by the equation:

$\Delta G = -nFE_{\text{cell}}$

Since $n$ (number of moles of electrons) and $F$ (Faraday's constant) are both positive quantities, for $\Delta G$ to be negative, the cell potential $E_{\text{cell}}$ must be positive, i.e., $E_{\text{cell}} > 0$.

questions.solution:

$2PbSO_4(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow Pb(s) + PbO_2(s) + 2H_2SO_4(aq)$

From this reaction, it is clear that $H_2SO_4$ is regenerated, which means the concentration of sulphuric acid in the electrolyte increases. Consequently, the density of the electrolyte solution also increases.

Lead sulphate ($PbSO_4$) is consumed from both electrodes, and the mass of the lead dioxide ($PbO_2$) electrode increases as it is formed at the positive electrode.

Answer: The concentration of sulphuric acid in the electrolyte increases.

questions.solution:
In a Leclanché dry cell, the anode is a zinc container and the cathode is a graphite rod. The graphite rod is surrounded by a mixture of powdered manganese dioxide ($\text{MnO}_2$) and carbon.

During the operation of the cell, hydrogen gas is produced at the cathode. If allowed to accumulate, it would cause polarization and a drop in voltage. The $\text{MnO}_2$ acts as a depolarizer by oxidizing the hydrogen to water, thereby preventing polarization.

The relevant cathode reaction is:
$\text{MnO}_2 + \text{NH}_4^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{MnO(OH)} + \text{NH}_3$

Thus, $\text{MnO}_2$ is the compound packed around the graphite rod to act as a depolarizer.

Answer: $\text{MnO}_2$

Consequently, the density of the electrolytic solution also decreases. Solid $\text{PbSO}_4$ is formed at both the anode and the cathode, not consumed. $\text{PbO}_2$ is consumed at the cathode, not formed at the anode.

For the cell reaction $M(s) + N^{2+}(aq) \rightleftharpoons M^{2+}(aq) + N(s)$, the equilibrium constant is $K_c$. The value of $\log K_c$ is ____.
(Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}$)
questions.question:
The standard reduction potentials of two metals $M$ and $N$ at $298\text{ K}$ are given below:
Half-Reaction$E^\circ$ at $298\text{ K}$
$M^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \rightarrow M(s)$$-0.440\text{ V}$
$N^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \rightarrow N(s)$$-0.145\text{ V}$

For the cell reaction $M(s) + N^{2+}(aq) \rightleftharpoons M^{2+}(aq) + N(s)$, the equilibrium constant is $K_c$. The value of $\log K_c$ is ____.
(Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}$)
questions.solution:
For the given cell reaction, $M$ undergoes oxidation and $N^{2+}$ undergoes reduction. Thus, $M$ acts as the anode and $N$ acts as the cathode.

The standard cell potential is given by:
$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}}$
$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{N^{2+}/N} - E^{\circ}_{M^{2+}/M}$
$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = -0.145 - (-0.440) = 0.295\text{ V}$

The number of electrons exchanged in the cell reaction is $n = 2$.

At equilibrium, the cell potential $E_{\text{cell}} = 0$. Using the Nernst equation:
$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = \dfrac{2.303 RT}{nF} \log K_c$

Substituting the given values:
$0.295 = \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log K_c$

$\log K_c = \dfrac{0.295 \times 2}{0.059}$

$\log K_c = \dfrac{0.590}{0.059} = 10$

Answer: $10$

questions.question:

(Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.059 \text{ V}$)
questions.solution:
For the given concentration cell, the cell reactions are:
Anode: $\text{Ag(s)} \rightarrow \text{Ag}^+_{\text{anode}} + e^-$
Cathode: $\text{Ag}^+_{\text{cathode}} + e^- \rightarrow \text{Ag(s)}$
Overall reaction: $\text{Ag}^+_{\text{cathode}} \rightarrow \text{Ag}^+_{\text{anode}}$

The standard cell potential for a concentration cell is $E^{\circ}_{cell} = 0 \text{ V}$.

Using the Nernst equation at $298 \text{ K}$:
$E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{n} \log \dfrac{[\text{Ag}^+]_{\text{anode}}}{[\text{Ag}^+]_{\text{cathode}}}$

Substituting the given values ($n = 1$, $E_{cell} = 0.236 \text{ V}$, $[\text{Ag}^+]_{\text{cathode}} = 0.01 \text{ M}$):
$0.236 = 0 - \dfrac{0.059}{1} \log \dfrac{[\text{Ag}^+]_{\text{anode}}}{10^{-2}}$

$\log \dfrac{[\text{Ag}^+]_{\text{anode}}}{10^{-2}} = -\dfrac{0.236}{0.059} = -4$

$\dfrac{[\text{Ag}^+]_{\text{anode}}}{10^{-2}} = 10^{-4}$

$[\text{Ag}^+]_{\text{anode}} = 10^{-6} \text{ M}$

In the anode compartment, the solution is saturated with $\text{AgBr}$. Let the solubility be $S$.
$[\text{Ag}^+] = [\text{Br}^-] = S = 10^{-6} \text{ M}$

The solubility product $K_{sp}$ of $\text{AgBr}$ is:
$K_{sp} = [\text{Ag}^+][\text{Br}^-] = (10^{-6})(10^{-6}) = 10^{-12}$

Comparing this with $1 \times 10^{-x}$, we get $x = 12$.

Answer: $12$

$\text{Pt}(s) | \text{H}_2(g, 4\text{ bar}) | \text{HCl}(aq, 1\text{ M}) | \text{H}_2(g, 0.1\text{ bar}) | \text{Pt}(s)$

Assuming that hydrogen behaves as an ideal gas, the cell potential is $x \times 10^{-3}\text{ V}$. The value of $x$ is ____.

questions.question:
Consider the following electrochemical cell at $298\text{ K}$:
$\text{Pt}(s) | \text{H}_2(g, 4\text{ bar}) | \text{HCl}(aq, 1\text{ M}) | \text{H}_2(g, 0.1\text{ bar}) | \text{Pt}(s)$

Assuming that hydrogen behaves as an ideal gas, the cell potential is $x \times 10^{-3}\text{ V}$. The value of $x$ is ____.
[Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.06\text{ V}$, $\log 2 = 0.3$]
questions.solution:
The given cell is a concentration cell. The half-cell reactions are:

Anode: $\text{H}_2(g, 4\text{ bar}) \rightarrow 2\text{H}^+(aq, 1\text{ M}) + 2e^-$
Cathode: $2\text{H}^+(aq, 1\text{ M}) + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2(g, 0.1\text{ bar})$

Overall cell reaction: $\text{H}_2(g, 4\text{ bar}) \rightarrow \text{H}_2(g, 0.1\text{ bar})$

The number of electrons transferred is $n = 2$. For a concentration cell, the standard cell potential $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 0\text{ V}$.

Using the Nernst equation:
$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{2.303 RT}{nF} \log Q$

Here, the reaction quotient $Q = \dfrac{P_{\text{H}_2(\text{cathode})}}{P_{\text{H}_2(\text{anode})}} = \dfrac{0.1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{40}$

Substituting the given values:
$E_{\text{cell}} = 0 - \dfrac{0.06}{2} \log\left(\dfrac{1}{40}\right)$

$E_{\text{cell}} = -0.03 \times (-\log 40)$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.03 \times (\log 4 + \log 10)$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.03 \times (2 \log 2 + 1)$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.03 \times (2 \times 0.3 + 1)$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.03 \times (0.6 + 1) = 0.03 \times 1.6$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.048\text{ V} = 48 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V}$

Comparing this with $x \times 10^{-3}\text{ V}$, we get $x = 48$.

Answer: $48$

options: The spontaneous reaction is $A + 2B^+ \rightarrow A^{2+} + 2B$ with $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.30$ V.
The spontaneous reaction is $A^{2+} + 2B \rightarrow A + 2B^+$ with $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.30$ V.
The spontaneous reaction is $A^{2+} + 2B \rightarrow A + 2B^+$ with $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.70$ V.
The spontaneous reaction is $A + 2B^+ \rightarrow A^{2+} + 2B$ with $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = -0.30$ V.
questions.solution:
Given standard reduction potentials:
$E^{\circ}_{A^{2+}|A} = 0.50 \text{ V}$
$E^{\circ}_{B^+|B} = 0.20 \text{ V}$

For a spontaneous reaction, the standard cell potential $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}$ must be positive. The species with the higher standard reduction potential will undergo reduction (act as the cathode), and the species with the lower standard reduction potential will undergo oxidation (act as the anode).

Since $E^{\circ}_{A^{2+}|A} > E^{\circ}_{B^+|B}$, $A^{2+}$ will be reduced and $B$ will be oxidized.

Reduction half-reaction (Cathode): $A^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow A$
Oxidation half-reaction (Anode): $2B \rightarrow 2B^+ + 2e^{-}$

Overall spontaneous cell reaction: $A^{2+} + 2B \rightarrow A + 2B^+$

The standard cell potential is calculated as:
$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}}$
$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 0.50 - 0.20 = 0.30 \text{ V}$

Answer: The spontaneous reaction is $A^{2+} + 2B \rightarrow A + 2B^+$ with $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.30$ V.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The EMF of the cell $\text{Cr} | \text{Cr}^{3+} (0.1 \text{ M}) || \text{Fe}^{2+} (0.01 \text{ M}) | \text{Fe}$ at $298 \text{ K}$ is $0.26 \text{ V}$. The equilibrium constant for the overall cell reaction is $10^x$. The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.06 \text{ V}$)
questions.question:
The EMF of the cell $\text{Cr} | \text{Cr}^{3+} (0.1 \text{ M}) || \text{Fe}^{2+} (0.01 \text{ M}) | \text{Fe}$ at $298 \text{ K}$ is $0.26 \text{ V}$. The equilibrium constant for the overall cell reaction is $10^x$. The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.06 \text{ V}$)
questions.solution:
The cell reaction is:
Anode: $\text{Cr} \rightarrow \text{Cr}^{3+} + 3e^{-}$
Cathode: $\text{Fe}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Fe}$

To balance the electrons, multiply the anode reaction by $2$ and the cathode reaction by $3$. The overall cell reaction is:
$2\text{Cr} + 3\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 3\text{Fe}$

The number of electrons transferred, $n = 6$.

The reaction quotient $Q$ is given by:
$Q = \dfrac{[\text{Cr}^{3+}]^2}{[\text{Fe}^{2+}]^3} = \dfrac{(0.1)^2}{(0.01)^3} = \dfrac{10^{-2}}{10^{-6}} = 10^4$

Using the Nernst equation:
$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{2.303 RT}{nF} \log Q$

Substituting the given values:
$0.26 = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0.06}{6} \log(10^4)$

$0.26 = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - 0.01 \times 4$

$0.26 = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - 0.04$

$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 0.30 \text{ V}$

At equilibrium, $E_{\text{cell}} = 0$ and $Q = K_{\text{eq}}$. The relation between $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}$ and $K_{\text{eq}}$ is:
$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = \dfrac{2.303 RT}{nF} \log K_{\text{eq}}$

$0.30 = \dfrac{0.06}{6} \log K_{\text{eq}}$

$0.30 = 0.01 \log K_{\text{eq}}$

$\log K_{\text{eq}} = \dfrac{0.30}{0.01} = 30$

$K_{\text{eq}} = 10^{30}$

Comparing with $K_{\text{eq}} = 10^x$, we get $x = 30$.

Answer: $30$

questions.question:

(Given: $\dfrac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.06\text{ V}$)
questions.solution:
The relation between the standard cell potential $E^{\circ}$ and the equilibrium constant $K_c$ is given by:

$E^{\circ} = \dfrac{2.303RT}{nF} \log K_c$

For the given cell reaction, the number of electrons transferred is $n = 2$.

Given $E^{\circ} = 1.20\text{ V}$ and $\dfrac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.06\text{ V}$.

Substituting the values into the equation:

$1.20 = \dfrac{0.06}{2} \log K_c$

$1.20 = 0.03 \log K_c$

$\log K_c = \dfrac{1.20}{0.03} = 40$

Answer: $40$

questions.question:

The standard cell potential ($E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}$) is $1.05 \text{ V}$ at $298 \text{ K}$. If the concentration of $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ is $0.1 \text{ M}$ and that of $\text{Ag}^{+}$ is $0.1 \text{ M}$, the cell potential is $x \times 10^{-2} \text{ V}$.
Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.06 \text{ V}$ at $298 \text{ K}$.
The value of $x$ is ____.
questions.solution:
The cell reaction is $\text{Ni(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Ni}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{Ag(s)}$

The number of electrons transferred in the reaction is $n = 2$.

Using the Nernst equation:

$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{2.303 RT}{nF} \log \dfrac{[\text{Ni}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^{+}]^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$E_{\text{cell}} = 1.05 - \dfrac{0.06}{2} \log \dfrac{0.1}{(0.1)^2}$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 1.05 - 0.03 \log \dfrac{0.1}{0.01}$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 1.05 - 0.03 \log 10$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 1.05 - 0.03(1)$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 1.02 \text{ V}$

Expressing the cell potential in the required format:

$E_{\text{cell}} = 102 \times 10^{-2} \text{ V}$

Comparing with $x \times 10^{-2} \text{ V}$, we get $x = 102$.

Answer: $102$

Consider the following galvanic cell:
$\text{Zn(s)} | \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq}) || \text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) | \text{Ag(s)}$
Which of the following changes will result in an increase in the cell potential ($E_{\text{cell}}$)?
questions.question:
Consider the following galvanic cell:
$\text{Zn(s)} | \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq}) || \text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) | \text{Ag(s)}$
Which of the following changes will result in an increase in the cell potential ($E_{\text{cell}}$)?
options: Increasing the mass of the $\text{Ag}$ electrode
questions.solution:
The overall cell reaction is:
$\text{Zn(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{Ag(s)}$

The Nernst equation for the cell potential is:
$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{2.303RT}{2F} \log \dfrac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^{+}]^2}$

To increase the cell potential $E_{\text{cell}}$, the value of the logarithmic term must decrease. This can be achieved by either decreasing the concentration of $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ ions or increasing the concentration of $\text{Ag}^{+}$ ions.

Changing the mass of solid electrodes ($\text{Ag}$ or $\text{Zn}$) does not affect the cell potential as their active masses are taken as unity.

Thus, decreasing the concentration of $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ ions will result in an increase in the cell potential.

Answer: Decreasing the concentration of $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ ions

When the concentration of $\text{Zn}^{2+}(aq)$ is $10^{-3}\text{ M}$ and that of $\text{Ni}^{2+}(aq)$ is $0.1\text{ M}$, the EMF of the cell becomes $E_2$. questions.question: The standard EMF of a galvanic cell involving the cell reaction $\text{Zn}(s) + \text{Ni}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Ni}(s)$ at $298\text{ K}$ is $E_1$. When the concentration of $\text{Zn}^{2+}(aq)$ is $10^{-3}\text{ M}$ and that of $\text{Ni}^{2+}(aq)$ is $0.1\text{ M}$, the EMF of the cell becomes $E_2$. The correct relationship between $E_1$ and $E_2$ is:
questions.solution:
The cell reaction is $\text{Zn}(s) + \text{Ni}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Ni}(s)$

The Nernst equation for the cell is given by:

$E = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n} \log \dfrac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ni}^{2+}]}$

Here, $n = 2$, $E^{\circ} = E_1$, and the new EMF is $E_2$.

Substituting the given concentrations, $[\text{Zn}^{2+}] = 10^{-3}\text{ M}$ and $[\text{Ni}^{2+}] = 0.1\text{ M}$:

$E_2 = E_1 - \dfrac{0.0591}{2} \log \dfrac{10^{-3}}{10^{-1}}$

$E_2 = E_1 - \dfrac{0.0591}{2} \log (10^{-2})$

$E_2 = E_1 - \dfrac{0.0591}{2} (-2)$

$E_2 = E_1 + 0.0591$

Since $0.0591 > 0$, it follows that $E_2 > E_1$, or $E_1 < E_2$.

Answer: $E_1 < E_2$

questions.question:
Consider the following electrochemical cell at $298 \text{ K}$:

$Pt(s) \mid H_2(g) (1 \text{ bar}) \mid \text{HCl}(aq) (0.001 \text{ M}) \parallel \text{HA}(aq) (0.1 \text{ M}) \mid H_2(g) (1 \text{ bar}) \mid Pt(s)$

Given that the $pK_a$ of the weak acid $\text{HA}$ is $5$, the measured EMF of this cell is zero. The correct reason for this observation is:
options: The molar concentrations of the acids in both half-cells are identical.
The pH of the solutions in both half-cells is exactly $3$.
Both half-cells function as standard hydrogen electrodes.
The weak acid $\text{HA}$ is completely ionized, neutralizing the cell potential.
questions.solution:
For the given concentration cell, the cell potential is given by the Nernst equation:

$E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{1} \log \dfrac{[H^+]_{anode}}{[H^+]_{cathode}}$

Since both electrodes are hydrogen electrodes, $E^{\circ}_{cell} = 0$. The measured EMF of the cell is zero, which implies:

$\log \dfrac{[H^+]_{anode}}{[H^+]_{cathode}} = 0 \Rightarrow [H^+]_{anode} = [H^+]_{cathode}$

In the anode half-cell, $\text{HCl}$ is a strong acid and dissociates completely. Thus, the hydrogen ion concentration is:

$[H^+]_{anode} = 0.001 \text{ M} = 10^{-3} \text{ M}$

The pH of the anode solution is:

$\text{pH}_{anode} = -\log(10^{-3}) = 3$

In the cathode half-cell, $\text{HA}$ is a weak acid with $pK_a = 5$, so $K_a = 10^{-5}$. The hydrogen ion concentration is given by:

$[H^+]_{cathode} = \sqrt{K_a \times C} = \sqrt{10^{-5} \times 0.1} = \sqrt{10^{-6}} = 10^{-3} \text{ M}$

The pH of the cathode solution is:

$\text{pH}_{cathode} = -\log(10^{-3}) = 3$

Since the pH of the solutions in both half-cells is exactly $3$, the hydrogen ion concentrations are equal, resulting in a zero cell potential.

Answer: The pH of the solutions in both half-cells is exactly $3$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The overall cell reaction for a galvanic cell is given as:
$\text{H}_2(g) + \text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2(s) \rightarrow 2\text{H}^+(aq) + 2\text{Cl}^-(aq) + 2\text{Hg}(l)$

Which of the following cell representations correctly corresponds to the above reaction?
questions.question:
The overall cell reaction for a galvanic cell is given as:
$\text{H}_2(g) + \text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2(s) \rightarrow 2\text{H}^+(aq) + 2\text{Cl}^-(aq) + 2\text{Hg}(l)$

Which of the following cell representations correctly corresponds to the above reaction?
questions.solution:
The given overall cell reaction is:

$\text{H}_2(g) + \text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2(s) \rightarrow 2\text{H}^+(aq) + 2\text{Cl}^-(aq) + 2\text{Hg}(l)$

The oxidation half-reaction occurs at the anode (left side):

$\text{H}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{H}^+(aq) + 2e^-$

The reduction half-reaction occurs at the cathode (right side):

$\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2(s) + 2e^- \rightarrow 2\text{Hg}(l) + 2\text{Cl}^-(aq)$

The anode consists of hydrogen gas bubbled over a platinum electrode in a solution containing $\text{H}^+$ ions. The cathode is a calomel electrode consisting of mercury, solid mercury(I) chloride, and a solution containing $\text{Cl}^-$ ions.

Since both electrodes require an aqueous solution containing $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, aqueous $\text{HCl}$ serves as the common electrolyte without the need for a salt bridge.

Combining the anode and cathode representations with the common electrolyte gives the cell notation:

$\text{Pt}(s) \mid \text{H}_2(g) \mid \text{HCl}(aq) \mid \text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2(s) \mid \text{Hg}(l)$

Answer: $\text{Pt}(s) \mid \text{H}_2(g) \mid \text{HCl}(aq) \mid \text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2(s) \mid \text{Hg}(l)$
questions.explanation:
The given overall cell reaction is:

$\text{H}_2(g) + \text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2(s) \rightarrow 2\text{H}^+(aq) + 2\text{Cl}^-(aq) + 2\text{Hg}(l)$

The reduction half-reaction occurs at the cathode (right side):

Since both electrodes require an aqueous solution containing $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, aqueous $\text{HCl}$ serves as the common electrolyte without the need for a salt bridge.

Combining the anode and cathode representations with the common electrolyte gives the cell notation:

$\text{Pt}(s) \mid \text{H}_2(g) \mid \text{HCl}(aq) \mid \text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2(s) \mid \text{Hg}(l)$

questions.solution:

Here, dichromate is reduced at the cathode and iron(II) is oxidized at the anode.

$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 1.33 - 0.77 = 0.56 \text{ V}$

The number of electrons transferred in the balanced chemical equation is $n = 6$.

The relationship between the standard cell potential and the equilibrium constant $K$ is given by the Nernst equation at equilibrium:

$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = \dfrac{2.303 RT}{nF} \log K$

Substituting the given values:

$0.56 = \dfrac{0.06}{6} \log K$

$0.56 = 0.01 \log K$

$\log K = \dfrac{0.56}{0.01} = 56$

$K = 10^{56}$

Comparing this with $K = 10^x$, we get $x = 56$.

Answer: $56$

An electrochemical cell is set up as follows:
$Pt(s) | Sn^{2+}(aq, 1\text{ M}), Sn^{4+}(aq, 1\text{ M}) || Fe^{3+}(aq, 1\text{ M}), Fe^{2+}(aq, 1\text{ M}) | Pt(s)$

Given: $E^\circ_{Sn^{4+}/Sn^{2+}} = +0.15\text{ V}$ and $E^\circ_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}} = +0.77\text{ V}$.

When the two electrodes are connected by an external wire, what is the direction of conventional current flow in the external circuit, and how does the cell potential change as the reaction proceeds?
questions.question:
An electrochemical cell is set up as follows:
$Pt(s) | Sn^{2+}(aq, 1\text{ M}), Sn^{4+}(aq, 1\text{ M}) || Fe^{3+}(aq, 1\text{ M}), Fe^{2+}(aq, 1\text{ M}) | Pt(s)$

Given: $E^\circ_{Sn^{4+}/Sn^{2+}} = +0.15\text{ V}$ and $E^\circ_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}} = +0.77\text{ V}$.

When the two electrodes are connected by an external wire, what is the direction of conventional current flow in the external circuit, and how does the cell potential change as the reaction proceeds?
options: From the $Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}$ electrode to the $Sn^{4+}/Sn^{2+}$ electrode, and the cell potential decreases.
From the $Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}$ electrode to the $Sn^{4+}/Sn^{2+}$ electrode, and the cell potential increases.
From the $Sn^{4+}/Sn^{2+}$ electrode to the $Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}$ electrode, and the cell potential decreases.
From the $Sn^{4+}/Sn^{2+}$ electrode to the $Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}$ electrode, and the cell potential increases.
questions.solution:
The standard reduction potential of the $Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}$ electrode ($+0.77\text{ V}$) is greater than that of the $Sn^{4+}/Sn^{2+}$ electrode ($+0.15\text{ V}$).

Thus, the $Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}$ electrode acts as the cathode (where reduction occurs) and the $Sn^{4+}/Sn^{2+}$ electrode acts as the anode (where oxidation occurs).

Electrons flow from the anode to the cathode in the external circuit, which means from the $Sn^{4+}/Sn^{2+}$ electrode to the $Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}$ electrode.

Conventional current flows in the direction opposite to the flow of electrons, i.e., from the $Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}$ electrode to the $Sn^{4+}/Sn^{2+}$ electrode.

As the cell reaction proceeds, reactants are consumed and products are formed. The reaction quotient $Q$ increases, and according to the Nernst equation, the cell potential $E_{cell}$ decreases until it reaches zero at equilibrium.

Answer: From the $Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}$ electrode to the $Sn^{4+}/Sn^{2+}$ electrode, and the cell potential decreases.

For the cell reaction at $298\text{ K}$:
$\text{H}_2(g, 1 \text{ bar}) + 2\text{AgCl}(s) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Ag}(s) + 2\text{H}^+(aq, 0.01 \text{ M}) + 2\text{Cl}^-(aq, 0.01 \text{ M})$
The standard Gibbs free energy change ($\Delta G^\circ$) is $-42460 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$. The EMF of the cell in which the given reaction takes place is $x \times 10^{-2} \text{ V}$.
The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: $1 \text{ F} = 96500 \text{ C mol}^{-1}$, $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.06 \text{ V}$)
questions.question:
For the cell reaction at $298\text{ K}$:
$\text{H}_2(g, 1 \text{ bar}) + 2\text{AgCl}(s) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Ag}(s) + 2\text{H}^+(aq, 0.01 \text{ M}) + 2\text{Cl}^-(aq, 0.01 \text{ M})$
The standard Gibbs free energy change ($\Delta G^\circ$) is $-42460 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$. The EMF of the cell in which the given reaction takes place is $x \times 10^{-2} \text{ V}$.
The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: $1 \text{ F} = 96500 \text{ C mol}^{-1}$, $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.06 \text{ V}$)
questions.solution:
The standard Gibbs free energy change is given by:

$\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}$

For the given cell reaction, the number of electrons transferred is $n = 2$.

Substituting the given values:

$-42460 = -2 \times 96500 \times E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$

$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \dfrac{42460}{2 \times 96500} = \dfrac{42460}{193000} = 0.22 \text{ V}$

The reaction quotient $Q$ for the cell reaction is:

$Q = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+]^2 [\text{Cl}^-]^2}{P_{\text{H}_2}}$

Given $[\text{H}^+] = 0.01 \text{ M} = 10^{-2} \text{ M}$, $[\text{Cl}^-] = 0.01 \text{ M} = 10^{-2} \text{ M}$, and $P_{\text{H}_2} = 1 \text{ bar}$:

$Q = \dfrac{(10^{-2})^2 (10^{-2})^2}{1} = 10^{-8}$

Using the Nernst equation to find the EMF of the cell:

$E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{2.303 RT}{nF} \log Q$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.22 - \dfrac{0.06}{2} \log(10^{-8})$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.22 - 0.03 \times (-8)$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.22 + 0.24 = 0.46 \text{ V}$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 46 \times 10^{-2} \text{ V}$

Comparing this with $x \times 10^{-2} \text{ V}$, we get $x = 46$.

Answer: $46$

The negative electrode is dipped in a solution having a hydrogen ion concentration of $10^{-6}\text{ M}$. If the electromotive force (EMF) of the cell is $0.177\text{ V}$, the concentration of hydrogen ions at the positive electrode is $10^{-x}\text{ M}$.
The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}$)
questions.question:
A galvanic cell is constructed using two hydrogen electrodes (at $1\text{ bar}$ pressure of $\text{H}_2$ gas) operating at $298\text{ K}$. The negative electrode is dipped in a solution having a hydrogen ion concentration of $10^{-6}\text{ M}$. If the electromotive force (EMF) of the cell is $0.177\text{ V}$, the concentration of hydrogen ions at the positive electrode is $10^{-x}\text{ M}$.
The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}$)
questions.solution:
For the given hydrogen concentration cell, the reactions at the electrodes are:

At anode (negative electrode): $\text{H}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow 2\text{H}^{+}(\text{anode}) + 2\text{e}^{-}$
At cathode (positive electrode): $2\text{H}^{+}(\text{cathode}) + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_2(\text{g})$

The overall cell reaction is:
$2\text{H}^{+}(\text{cathode}) \rightarrow 2\text{H}^{+}(\text{anode})$

Applying the Nernst equation for the cell at $298\text{ K}$:
$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log \dfrac{[\text{H}^{+}]_{\text{anode}}^2}{[\text{H}^{+}]_{\text{cathode}}^2}$

For a concentration cell, $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 0$. Simplifying the equation gives:
$E_{\text{cell}} = -0.059 \log \dfrac{[\text{H}^{+}]_{\text{anode}}}{[\text{H}^{+}]_{\text{cathode}}}$

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0.059 \log \dfrac{[\text{H}^{+}]_{\text{cathode}}}{[\text{H}^{+}]_{\text{anode}}}$

Substituting the given values $E_{\text{cell}} = 0.177\text{ V}$, $[\text{H}^{+}]_{\text{anode}} = 10^{-6}\text{ M}$, and $[\text{H}^{+}]_{\text{cathode}} = 10^{-x}\text{ M}$:
$0.177 = 0.059 \log \dfrac{10^{-x}}{10^{-6}}$

$\dfrac{0.177}{0.059} = \log (10^{6-x})$

$3 = 6 - x$

$x = 3$

Answer: $3$

$\text{Br}_2 (\text{l}) + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Br}^- (\text{aq})$$1.07$
The standard reduction potential $E^\circ$ for the half-reaction $2\text{BrO}^- (\text{aq}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} (\text{l}) + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 (\text{l}) + 4\text{OH}^- (\text{aq})$ is $x \times 10^{-2}$ V. The value of $x$ is ____.
questions.solution:
The given half-reactions are:

(i) $\text{BrO}^- (\text{aq}) + \text{H}_2\text{O} (\text{l}) + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Br}^- (\text{aq}) + 2\text{OH}^- (\text{aq})$
$\Delta G_1^\circ = -n_1FE_1^\circ = -2F(0.76)$

(ii) $\text{Br}_2 (\text{l}) + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Br}^- (\text{aq})$
$\Delta G_2^\circ = -n_2FE_2^\circ = -2F(1.07)$

The target half-reaction is:
(iii) $2\text{BrO}^- (\text{aq}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} (\text{l}) + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 (\text{l}) + 4\text{OH}^- (\text{aq})$

Reaction (iii) can be obtained by multiplying reaction (i) by $2$ and subtracting reaction (ii):
$\Delta G_3^\circ = 2\Delta G_1^\circ - \Delta G_2^\circ$

Substituting the values of $\Delta G^\circ$:
$-n_3FE_3^\circ = 2[-2F(0.76)] - [-2F(1.07)]$

Since the number of electrons involved in the target reaction is $n_3 = 2$:
$-2FE_3^\circ = -4F(0.76) + 2F(1.07)$

Dividing the entire equation by $-2F$:
$E_3^\circ = 2(0.76) - 1.07$
$E_3^\circ = 1.52 - 1.07 = 0.45 \text{ V}$

Expressing this in the required format:
$E_3^\circ = 45 \times 10^{-2} \text{ V}$

Therefore, the value of $x$ is $45$.

Answer: $45$

$R \rightarrow R^{3+} + 3e^-$$-1.40$
$S^{4+} + 2e^- \rightarrow S^{2+}$$+0.15$

questions.question:
Given below are the standard electrode potentials of some half-cell reactions:
Half-cell reaction$E^{\circ}$ (V)
$P \rightarrow P^{2+} + 2e^-$$+2.90$
$Q^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Q$$-0.40$
$R \rightarrow R^{3+} + 3e^-$$-1.40$
$S^{4+} + 2e^- \rightarrow S^{2+}$$+0.15$
The maximum standard cell potential that can be obtained by constructing a galvanic cell from any two of the above half-cells is $x \times 10^{-1}$ V. The value of $x$ is ____.
questions.solution:
To find the maximum standard cell potential, we first convert all the given potentials into standard reduction potentials ($E^{\circ}_{red}$):

1. $P \rightarrow P^{2+} + 2e^-$, $E^{\circ}_{ox} = +2.90$ V $\Rightarrow E^{\circ}_{red} = -2.90$ V
2. $Q^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Q$, $E^{\circ}_{red} = -0.40$ V
3. $R \rightarrow R^{3+} + 3e^-$, $E^{\circ}_{ox} = -1.40$ V $\Rightarrow E^{\circ}_{red} = +1.40$ V
4. $S^{4+} + 2e^- \rightarrow S^{2+}$, $E^{\circ}_{red} = +0.15$ V

The standard cell potential for a galvanic cell is given by:
$E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode}$

To obtain the maximum standard cell potential, we must select the half-cell with the highest standard reduction potential as the cathode and the half-cell with the lowest standard reduction potential as the anode.

Highest $E^{\circ}_{red}$ (Cathode) = $+1.40$ V (for $R^{3+}/R$)
Lowest $E^{\circ}_{red}$ (Anode) = $-2.90$ V (for $P^{2+}/P$)

Maximum $E^{\circ}_{cell} = 1.40 - (-2.90) = 1.40 + 2.90 = 4.30$ V

We are given that the maximum standard cell potential is $x \times 10^{-1}$ V.
Therefore, $4.30 = x \times 10^{-1}$
$x = 43$

Answer: $43$

Given below are two statements:
Statement I: In an electrolytic cell, external electrical energy is used to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction.
Statement II: The anode is negatively charged in an electrolytic cell, whereas it is positively charged in a galvanic cell.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: In an electrolytic cell, external electrical energy is used to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction.
Statement II: The anode is negatively charged in an electrolytic cell, whereas it is positively charged in a galvanic cell.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution:
Statement I is correct because an electrolytic cell converts external electrical energy into chemical energy to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction.

Statement II is incorrect because in an electrolytic cell, the anode is connected to the positive terminal of the external battery and is positively charged. In contrast, in a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the anode, releasing electrons and making it negatively charged.

questions.solution:
In the first cell with nickel electrodes, nickel acts as an active electrode. The oxidation potential of nickel is higher than that of water and chloride ions. Hence, the nickel anode undergoes oxidation to form $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ions.

In the second cell with platinum electrodes, platinum acts as an inert electrode. The competing oxidation reactions at the anode are the oxidation of water to oxygen gas and the oxidation of chloride ions to chlorine gas. Although the standard oxidation potential of water is slightly higher than that of chloride ions, the oxidation of water requires a high overpotential. Therefore, chloride ions are preferentially oxidized to chlorine gas.

The aqueous solution of $\text{NaCl}$ contains $\text{Na}^+$, $\text{Cl}^-$, $\text{H}^+$, and $\text{OH}^-$ ions.

At the mercury cathode, the discharge of $\text{H}^+$ ions requires a high overvoltage. Additionally, sodium forms an amalgam with mercury, which lowers the discharge potential of $\text{Na}^+$. Therefore, $\text{Na}^+$ ions are preferentially discharged at the cathode instead of $\text{H}^+$ ions.

At the inert anode, the discharge potential of $\text{Cl}^-$ is lower than that of $\text{OH}^-$ due to the overvoltage of oxygen. Thus, $\text{Cl}^-$ ions are preferentially discharged at the anode.

The primary ions discharged are $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$.

Answer: $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$

questions.question: Two electrolytic cells, A and B, containing an alkaline solution of cuprous cyanide and an acidified solution of copper(II) sulphate respectively, are connected in series. A steady current is passed through the cells for a certain duration. The ratio of the mass of copper deposited at the cathode of cell A to the mass of copper deposited at the cathode of cell B is ____.
questions.solution:
In cell A, the electrolyte is cuprous cyanide, where copper is in the $+1$ oxidation state. The reduction reaction at the cathode is:

$\text{Cu}^{+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu}$

The equivalent weight of copper in cell A is $E_A = \dfrac{M}{1} = M$, where $M$ is the molar mass of copper.

In cell B, the electrolyte is copper(II) sulphate, where copper is in the $+2$ oxidation state. The reduction reaction at the cathode is:

$\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu}$

The equivalent weight of copper in cell B is $E_B = \dfrac{M}{2}$.

Since the cells are connected in series, the same amount of charge passes through both cells. According to Faraday's second law of electrolysis, the mass of a substance deposited is directly proportional to its equivalent weight.

$\dfrac{m_A}{m_B} = \dfrac{E_A}{E_B} = \dfrac{M}{M/2} = 2$

Answer: $2$

$\text{Cu}^{+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu}$

$\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu}$

The equivalent weight of copper in cell B is $E_B = \dfrac{M}{2}$.

$\dfrac{m_A}{m_B} = \dfrac{E_A}{E_B} = \dfrac{M}{M/2} = 2$

Answer: $2$

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding Faraday's laws of electrolysis:
(A) The electrochemical equivalent of a substance is independent of the temperature and concentration of the electrolyte.
(B) Faraday's laws hold true whether the electrodes used are inert or active.
(C) Faraday's laws fail if a mixture of multiple electrolytes is present in the solution.
(D) These laws are strictly valid only when the conduction of current through the electrolyte is purely ionic.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Statement (A): The electrochemical equivalent $Z = \dfrac{E}{F}$, where $E$ is the equivalent weight of the substance. It is a constant for a given substance undergoing a specific reaction and is independent of temperature and concentration. Thus, (A) is correct.

Statement (B): Faraday's laws apply to both inert and active electrodes. For active electrodes, the mass of the electrode dissolved or deposited is still strictly proportional to the charge passed. Thus, (B) is correct.

Statement (C): If a mixture of multiple electrolytes is present, the total number of equivalents of all substances discharged at an electrode is exactly equal to the number of Faradays of charge passed. Faraday's laws remain valid for the total chemical change. Thus, (C) is incorrect.

Statement (D): If the electrolyte exhibits any electronic conduction, a portion of the current will pass without causing any chemical change at the electrodes, leading to an apparent deviation from Faraday's laws. Therefore, the laws are strictly valid only when the conduction is purely ionic. Thus, (D) is correct.

The correct statements are (A), (B), and (D).

Answer: (A), (B) and (D) only

If $0.8 \text{ g}$ of hydrogen gas is liberated at the cathode of the first cell, the mass of copper deposited at the cathode of the second cell is $x \times 10^{-1} \text{ g}$.
The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: Molar masses of $\text{H}$ and $\text{Cu}$ are $1 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and $63.5 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ respectively)
questions.question:
A constant electric current was passed through two electrolytic cells connected in series, one containing an aqueous solution of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and the other containing an aqueous solution of $\text{CuSO}_4$. If $0.8 \text{ g}$ of hydrogen gas is liberated at the cathode of the first cell, the mass of copper deposited at the cathode of the second cell is $x \times 10^{-1} \text{ g}$.
The value of $x$ is ____.
(Given: Molar masses of $\text{H}$ and $\text{Cu}$ are $1 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and $63.5 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ respectively)
questions.solution:
According to Faraday's second law of electrolysis, when the same quantity of electricity is passed through different electrolytes connected in series, the masses of the substances deposited or liberated at the electrodes are directly proportional to their equivalent weights.

$\dfrac{W_{\text{H}_2}}{E_{\text{H}}} = \dfrac{W_{\text{Cu}}}{E_{\text{Cu}}}$

Given $W_{\text{H}_2} = 0.8 \text{ g}$

Equivalent weight of hydrogen, $E_{\text{H}} = \dfrac{1}{1} = 1 \text{ g eq}^{-1}$

Equivalent weight of copper, $E_{\text{Cu}} = \dfrac{63.5}{2} = 31.75 \text{ g eq}^{-1}$

Substituting the values:

$\dfrac{0.8}{1} = \dfrac{W_{\text{Cu}}}{31.75}$

$W_{\text{Cu}} = 0.8 \times 31.75 = 25.4 \text{ g}$

The mass of copper deposited is given as $x \times 10^{-1} \text{ g}$.

$25.4 = x \times 10^{-1} \Rightarrow x = 254$

Answer: $254$

A current of $2.5\text{ A}$ is passed through an aqueous solution of $\text{Cr}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$ for $193$ minutes. The mass of chromium deposited at the cathode is $4.42\text{ g}$. The current efficiency of the electrodeposition process is ____ %. (Nearest integer)

questions.question:
A current of $2.5\text{ A}$ is passed through an aqueous solution of $\text{Cr}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$ for $193$ minutes. The mass of chromium deposited at the cathode is $4.42\text{ g}$. The current efficiency of the electrodeposition process is ____ %. (Nearest integer)

(Given: Molar mass of $\text{Cr} = 52\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, $1\text{ F} = 96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
The total charge passed through the solution is given by $Q = I \times t$

$Q = 2.5 \times 193 \times 60 = 28950\text{ C}$

The reduction reaction of chromium at the cathode is:

$\text{Cr}^{3+} + 3e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cr}$

The theoretical mass of chromium deposited can be calculated using Faraday's law of electrolysis:

$W_{\text{theoretical}} = \dfrac{M \times Q}{n \times F}$

$W_{\text{theoretical}} = \dfrac{52 \times 28950}{3 \times 96500} = \dfrac{52 \times 28950}{289500} = 5.2\text{ g}$

The current efficiency is the ratio of the actual mass deposited to the theoretical mass deposited:

$\text{Current efficiency} = \dfrac{W_{\text{actual}}}{W_{\text{theoretical}}} \times 100$

$\text{Current efficiency} = \dfrac{4.42}{5.2} \times 100 = 85\%$

Answer: $85$

During the electrolysis of a dilute aqueous solution of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, water is oxidized at the anode and hydrogen ions are reduced at the cathode.

At the anode (oxidation):
$2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{O}_2(g) + 4\text{H}^+(aq) + 4e^-$

At the cathode (reduction):
$2\text{H}^+(aq) + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2(g)$

To balance the electrons, we multiply the cathode reaction by 2:
$4\text{H}^+(aq) + 4e^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2(g)$

For every $4$ moles of electrons ($4\text{F}$ of charge) passed through the solution:
Moles of $\text{O}_2$ gas liberated at the anode = $1$
Mass of $\text{O}_2$ ($m_A$) = $1 \times 32 = 32 \text{ g}$

Moles of $\text{H}_2$ gas liberated at the cathode = $2$
Mass of $\text{H}_2$ ($m_C$) = $2 \times 2 = 4 \text{ g}$

The ratio of the mass of the gas liberated at the anode to the mass of the gas liberated at the cathode is:
$\dfrac{m_A}{m_C} = \dfrac{32}{4} = 8$

Answer: $8$

questions.q: Two different substances have electrochemical equivalents $Z_1$ and $Z_2$, respectively. If the same mass of each substance is to be deposited at the respective electrodes in the same time interval, the ratio of the currents ($I_1 : I_2$) passed through their solutions must be:
questions.question: Two different substances have electrochemical equivalents $Z_1$ and $Z_2$, respectively. If the same mass of each substance is to be deposited at the respective electrodes in the same time interval, the ratio of the currents ($I_1 : I_2$) passed through their solutions must be:
questions.solution:
According to Faraday's first law of electrolysis, the mass $m$ of a substance deposited at an electrode is given by $m = ZIt$, where $Z$ is the electrochemical equivalent, $I$ is the current, and $t$ is the time.

For the two substances, the masses deposited are $m_1 = Z_1 I_1 t$ and $m_2 = Z_2 I_2 t$.

Given that the same mass is deposited in the same time interval, $m_1 = m_2$.

$Z_1 I_1 t = Z_2 I_2 t$

$Z_1 I_1 = Z_2 I_2$

$\dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = \dfrac{Z_2}{Z_1}$

Thus, the ratio of the currents is $Z_2 : Z_1$.

Answer: $Z_2 : Z_1$

questions.question: An identical quantity of electric charge is passed through two separate electrolytic cells containing $1\text{ M } \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(\text{aq})$ and $1\text{ M } \text{HCl}(\text{aq})$ respectively, using inert electrodes. The ratio of the number of moles of hydrogen gas evolved at the cathode in the two cells ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 : \text{HCl}$) is:
questions.solution:
At the cathode, the reduction of hydrogen ions takes place in both the acidic solutions.

The reaction is given by:

$2H^{+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow H_2(g)$

According to Faraday's law of electrolysis, the number of moles of a substance deposited or evolved at an electrode is given by:

$n = \dfrac{Q}{zF}$

where $Q$ is the charge passed, $z$ is the number of electrons involved per mole of the product, and $F$ is Faraday's constant.

For the evolution of one mole of $H_2$ gas, $2$ moles of electrons are required, so $z = 2$.

Since an identical quantity of charge $Q$ is passed through both the cells, the number of moles of $H_2$ gas evolved in both cells will be:

$n = \dfrac{Q}{2F}$

Thus, the number of moles of hydrogen gas evolved in both cells is the same, and the ratio is $1 : 1$.

Answer: $1 : 1$

questions.question: During the electrolysis of an acidified aqueous solution of $\text{AgNO}_3$ using inert platinum electrodes, which of the following represents the primary reaction occurring at the anode?
questions.solution:
During the electrolysis of an acidified aqueous solution of $\text{AgNO}_3$ using inert platinum electrodes, oxidation occurs at the anode.

The species present near the anode are $\text{NO}_3^-$ ions and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules. Since platinum is an inert electrode, it does not undergo oxidation.

The standard oxidation potential of water is higher than that of the nitrate ion ($\text{NO}_3^-$). Therefore, water is preferentially oxidized at the anode to release oxygen gas.

The oxidation reaction at the anode is:
$2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{O}_2(g) + 4\text{H}^+(aq) + 4e^-$

After prolonged electrolysis, the blue colour of the solution is completely discharged and a colourless solution remains, along with the evolution of a gas at the anode. The final colourless solution is essentially an aqueous solution of:
questions.question: An aqueous solution of $\text{CuSO}_4$ is electrolysed using inert platinum electrodes. After prolonged electrolysis, the blue colour of the solution is completely discharged and a colourless solution remains, along with the evolution of a gas at the anode. The final colourless solution is essentially an aqueous solution of:
questions.solution:
During the electrolysis of aqueous $\text{CuSO}_4$ using inert platinum electrodes, the following reactions occur:

At cathode: $\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Cu(s)}$

At anode: $2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{O}_2\text{(g)} + 4\text{H}^+\text{(aq)} + 4\text{e}^-$

The blue colour of the solution is due to $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions. Upon prolonged electrolysis, all $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions are deposited at the cathode as solid copper, causing the blue colour to completely discharge.

At the anode, oxygen gas is evolved and $\text{H}^+$ ions are released into the solution. The $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ions remain unchanged in the solution.

Thus, the final colourless solution contains $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ions, which is essentially an aqueous solution of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.

Answer: $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$

Ion$E^{\circ} (\text{V})$

$\text{Ni}^{2+}$$-0.25$

As the applied voltage is gradually increased, which of the following represents the correct sequence of deposition of metals on the cathode?
questions.question:
An aqueous solution containing $1.0\text{ M}$ each of $\text{AgNO}_3$, $\text{Cu(NO}_3)_2$, $\text{Ni(NO}_3)_2$, and $\text{Al(NO}_3)_3$ is subjected to electrolysis using inert platinum electrodes. The standard reduction potentials of the relevant metal ions are given below:

Ion$E^{\circ} (\text{V})$
$\text{Ag}^{+}$$+0.80$
$\text{Cu}^{2+}$$+0.34$
$\text{Ni}^{2+}$$-0.25$
$\text{Al}^{3+}$$-1.66$


As the applied voltage is gradually increased, which of the following represents the correct sequence of deposition of metals on the cathode?
questions.solution:
The deposition of metals at the cathode during electrolysis depends on their standard reduction potentials. The species with the higher reduction potential is reduced preferentially.

The given standard reduction potentials are:
$E^{\circ}_{\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}$
$E^{\circ}_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}$
$E^{\circ}_{\text{Ni}^{2+}/\text{Ni}} = -0.25\text{ V}$
$E^{\circ}_{\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al}} = -1.66\text{ V}$

The standard reduction potential of water to hydrogen gas is $-0.83\text{ V}$.

Arranging the reducible species in decreasing order of their reduction potentials:
$\text{Ag}^{+} > \text{Cu}^{2+} > \text{Ni}^{2+} > \text{H}_2\text{O} > \text{Al}^{3+}$

As the applied voltage is increased, $\text{Ag}^{+}$ is reduced first, followed by $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, and then $\text{Ni}^{2+}$.

Since the reduction potential of $\text{Al}^{3+}$ is much lower than that of water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ will be reduced to $\text{H}_2$ gas at the cathode before $\text{Al}^{3+}$ can be reduced. Therefore, $\text{Al}$ metal will not be deposited from the aqueous solution.

The correct sequence of deposition is $\text{Ag}, \text{Cu}, \text{Ni}$.

Answer: $\text{Ag}, \text{Cu}, \text{Ni}$
